records.name: The Price of Our Inheritance
records.description: Vincent Erie inherited a claim to Verenia, unpaid suppliers and a frontier where every repaired bridge might become tomorrow's battlefield. Iovinus Eyrie's ancestry offers an answer as convincing as his own. Before choosing a settlement with his cousin or a campaign against him, Vincent must hear what either course will ask of the country that pays for it.
records.brief: An unpaid supplier's coin tray beside a splintered bridge beam and an ancestral claim scroll.

records.name: An Inheritance We Can Share
records.description: Vincent can keep his claim to Verenia without making every neighbour live beneath the threat of his army. He will seek a settlement with Eyrie: hear the country, let the family speak, and accept guarantees that bind his own officers before asking Iovinus to disarm the feud. This choice closes the road to imposing his inheritance by conquest. If the other court refuses, Erie must still have a future worth building.
records.brief: Two independent gate keys resting equally on a negotiation table, a sheathed sword below.

records.name: A Hearing for the Living
records.description: Petitions arrive wrapped in deeds, casualty notices and invoices that nobody expects to be paid. Their authors have practical questions for the duke: when may a cart cross the border, who repairs a ruined workshop, and where is a missing brother? Receiving them in public would make their demands harder to forget. Receiving them privately would leave more room for the court to bargain.
records.brief: A public petition box containing a property sketch, with a damaged cart wheel beside it.

records.name: Kinship Beyond the Feud
records.description: Rosaline Erie of Bantry and Montague Eyrie, Earl of Verenia, have kept a personal connection alive where their elders see only competing claims. Lady Katrina is aunt to both dukes; the family knows how to reach the other court without bringing an ultimatum. Vincent will protect that opening, not purchase it with a marriage promise. The first people allowed across the boundary must be free to speak for themselves.
records.brief: Two personal envelopes crossing an open family gate; no marriage ring or betrothal seal.

records.name: Silence Along the Frontier
records.description: The grievances have been heard, the families have spoken and the safeguards have been chosen. Now Vincent must make restraint an order his captains cannot mistake for a pause before the next raid. Patrols will cease crossing the line to seize cattle or settle an old insult. This armistice will hold while the Houses build a permanent settlement, without an anniversary telling their officers to resume the feud.
records.brief: A frontier patrol barrier lowered across a raiding path, with both service rifles laid at rest.

records.name: The First Cart Across
records.description: A barricade can be removed in an afternoon. A damaged culvert, a disputed toll and a carrier who has lost three carts require more work. Engineers and local officials will reopen the roads of our own territory while the ceasefire holds. Each ordinary journey completed safely will make the next agreement a little less difficult to imagine.
records.brief: A laden cart crossing a freshly repaired culvert beneath a raised toll arm.

records.name: The Price of Restraint
records.description: The petitioners want more than a promise that this season will be different. A farmer asks who will stop the next patrol; a dispossessed family asks who will answer for the last one. After hearing them and establishing contact across the family divide, Vincent must put something of his own behind the peace. Joint patrols would expose his officers to scrutiny. A restitution fund would oblige his court to acknowledge damage done in his name. He cannot demand a concession while refusing every cost of his own.
records.brief: A restitution coin chest beside paired patrol lanterns, two possible costs of credible restraint.

records.name: The Treaty of Friendship
records.description: The reopened crossing has given both courts something their genealogists could not: an example of life without the feud. The treaty will turn that experience into a settlement. Vincent and Iovinus relinquish their demands upon each other's lands and end the privileges that kept the quarrel alive. Neither receives a defeated cousin's submission. Each receives a neighbour whose independence is no longer an unfinished war.
records.brief: Two rival boundary stakes laid down beside an open crossing and balanced treaty clasps.

records.name: Who Speaks at the Congress?
records.description: The court can appoint household delegates who know every title and precedence. Towns and parishes can send representatives who know which bridge still needs timber. Giving the latter a place will consume political capital and complicate bargaining, but their participation can give an equal council a public purpose beyond accommodating two dynasties.
records.brief: A modest town delegate's chair drawn up beside a formal congress lectern.

records.name: An Intergigantes Association
records.description: Katrina's council chose to work between the giants, not to shut its doors. Offer Avian a treaty that makes cooperation the first step towards a common state. Its municipal charters and colleges must have a place in the eventual constitution. The first signature opens that work; only a later accession act can transfer sovereignty.
records.brief: An association invitation case resting beside an unoccupied Avian chair, before any transfer of sovereignty.
records.lore_notes: Localization aliases resolve to the older invitation; this distinct active focus invokes HSM_VER_AVR_offer. Association is not incorporation.

records.brief: An Avian college key placed beside two municipal charter bindings at an open treaty table.

records.name: A Charter of Agreed Powers
records.description: The treaty has quieted the frontier; it has not decided who may speak for a common court, a shared workshop or the next dispute between the Houses. With delegates appointed and Avian offered a seat, Vincent must put a constitution before the congress. An equal council gives each partner the same standing. A limited ducal presidency promises continuity, but asks his cousin to accept a chair that Vincent alone would occupy. The peace is already real. The question is what they will build upon it.
records.brief: A constitutional binding held by equal clasps beside a detachable presiding chair, powers still under negotiation.

records.name: Orders the Other Side Can Read
records.description: The quartermasters have discovered that their supply returns describe the same shortages in incompatible columns. A joint staff will bring the returns, maps and exercise plans to one table. Officers must learn to ask for another House's cooperation without mistaking a colleague's signature for authority over his troops.
records.brief: Two incompatible supply charts aligned beneath one field ruler and a staff telephone.

records.name: Standards Across the Border
records.description: A replacement part should fit regardless of which House paid for it. Engineers will compare drawings, test each other's measurements and take the disputed pieces back to the workshops. The common technical offices must earn their authority at a workbench, where a seal cannot conceal a badly cut thread.
records.brief: A threaded bolt from one workshop fitting a nut from another beneath a shared caliper.

records.name: A Judgement Against the Duke
records.description: Our common court has received a claim to an estate promised to one of Vincent's own veterans and patrons. The former owners belong to a family divided by the old battle lines. Their documents are sound. The charter will mean little unless its judgement can reach a beneficiary of the duke's personal word.
records.brief: Justice scales holding an estate key above a veteran's sheathed sword, law reaching a ducal patron.

records.name: An Agreement to Stand Together
records.description: Staff cooperation can prepare a defence, but only a further agreement can commit the Houses to a military league. We shall develop support methods and offer Eyrie a defensive partnership where existing commitments permit it. Avian, if a charter partner, will receive its own invitation. Each government must consent to the obligations it takes on.
records.brief: Two defensive lanterns joined by a signal cable beside an unopened invitation for a third partner.

records.name: Finish the Work We Promised
records.description: The first petitions were about livelihoods, not constitutional diagrams. We must complete the works promised at home, bringing new civilian production into service where we still hold our territory. The public commitments can then be discharged. Those who asked the duke for help deserve something more substantial than a copy of the charter.
records.brief: A completed civilian workshop with its final repair scaffold being removed.

records.name: A Generation Without the Feud
records.description: The union will be judged by the habits it makes possible: a court obeyed, a consignment delivered, a dispute settled without calling the reserves. Vincent has not forgotten his inheritance. He is learning what authority becomes when others accept its exercise and can hold it to its word. Let that be the settlement the next generation receives.
records.brief: A repaired market bridge carrying a school satchel and trade crate, peace becoming everyday habit.

records.name: The Country We Can Rebuild
records.description: The shared settlement has failed, whether at the first safeguards or at the final charter. A refusal cannot be signed away, and a fallen neighbouring government cannot keep a dead ruler's promises. Vincent can still keep his own: the schools, workshops and roads will not wait for another congress. Whatever agreements remain valid will be respected. Whatever was never agreed will not be invented. We chose negotiation, not an invasion postponed until an unwelcome answer.
records.brief: A domestic school roof being repaired beside a closed unused congress invitation.

records.name: The Work of Reconstruction
records.description: Neglected bridges, leaking roofs and unanswered petitions have become ordinary features of life in Erie. We will establish a small reconstruction office to survey the damage, arrange deliveries and give local repair crews a reliable point of contact. Its authority will rest on work completed.
records.brief: A surveyor's level above a roof beam and an organised repair-material crate.

records.name: Restore Public Services
records.description: Clean wells, working dispensaries and dependable local offices matter to families long before grand plans reach them. Repair crews will restore these services first, while regular inspections keep them from falling into neglect again. A household should not have to spend its last savings on failures the administration could have prevented.
records.brief: A restored village well beside a medicine cabinet and maintenance wrench.

records.name: Reopen the District Roads
records.description: The roads of Erie, Balefire and Comrick must carry grain, tools and travellers in every season. Repaired bridges, drainage ditches and maintained surfaces will reconnect isolated settlements with their markets. The engineers' surveys will also guide our next construction projects.
records.brief: A three-way district road junction with repaired drainage and a small bridge.

records.name: A Civilian Industrial Base
records.description: Our builders need reliable supplies of timber, fittings and machine parts. Expanding civilian production will give local firms steady contracts and put more of that work within reach. This is one step towards an industrial economy, with much still to be built.
records.brief: A civilian machine shop producing construction fittings beside timber stacks.

records.name: Connect the Workshops
records.description: A workshop can grow beyond its founder's tools when it can order standard parts and train apprentices to use them. We will expand manufacturing premises and bring willing workshops into a common system of measurements, inspections and orders. Small producers will retain their craft while learning to supply a larger market.
records.brief: A common drive shaft joining several small workshop benches.

records.name: A Trade After Service
records.description: Returning soldiers bring practical skills, but a service record is no guarantee of a livelihood. A new placement scheme will match veterans with apprenticeships, repair crews and workshop jobs, with suitable work for those carrying lasting injuries. Experienced volunteers can also help prepare the next intake of recruits.
records.brief: A worn service helmet hung above an apprentice's new tool apron.

records.name: Schools Within Reach
records.description: Children should not lose their chance to learn because the nearest classroom is a day's journey away. We will reopen neglected rooms, provide basic books and offer evening lessons to adults. Reading, arithmetic and an introduction to practical science will make further study possible for more households.
records.brief: A modest village classroom desk with an illustrated primer and an evening lamp.

records.name: Train the Teachers
records.description: Opening a classroom is easier than finding someone prepared to teach in it. New teacher courses will combine supervised lessons with arithmetic, record keeping and elementary technical subjects. Graduates will return to local schools with materials they can use and colleagues they can consult.
records.brief: An instructor's demonstration slate carrying a geometric lesson beside a prepared teaching box.

records.name: Found a Technical College
records.description: With schools and civilian workshops in place, we can establish a modest technical college. Its first laboratories will teach mechanics and electrical measurement, while workshop placements keep instruction close to practical problems. This new institution will give Erie's growing scientific community a place to train its successors.
records.brief: A college laboratory arch framing an electrical meter and a mechanical teaching model.

records.name: From Lessons to Research
records.description: The college can now support a small team working on problems beyond the classroom. A functioning civilian industrial base and an understanding of electrical engineering will let researchers build instruments, test designs and record results. Sustained research needs a budget, equipment and time as well as promising ideas.
records.brief: A precision electrical test bench with a notebook showing measured curves.

records.name: Coordinate Research
records.description: Our expanding factories and trained workforce can sustain a broader scientific programme. We will form a small research council to share laboratory time, award practical commissions and publish useful findings. Once basic machine tools and construction methods are established, a second permanent research team can begin work.
records.brief: A laboratory scheduling dial between two different research instruments and a shared equipment key.

records.name: Books Beyond the Classroom
records.description: School leavers need somewhere to keep learning. Public reading rooms will lend practical manuals, newspapers and stories, while travelling librarians carry books to settlements too small to maintain a collection of their own.
records.brief: A travelling book chest opened beside a public reading-room lamp.

records.name: A Place for Every Pupil
records.description: A school is public only when every family can use it. Attendance officers will work with parents, teachers and employers to bring missing pupils into class, and adult tutors will welcome those whose childhood passed without that chance.
records.brief: An open school gate with several differently sized satchels arranged along its welcoming path.

records.name: Homes Fit for Work and Rest
records.description: Crowded lodgings and leaking roofs consume the wages that should keep a household secure. District builders will repair rented homes and lay out affordable housing near the workshops, with residents able to demand repairs without risking eviction.
records.brief: A repaired row-house roof above a sound window and a mason's trowel.

records.name: Security Through Hard Times
records.description: Illness and injury should not send a working family back to the poorhouse. Employers, workers and the treasury will sustain an insurance fund whose local offices pay claims promptly and answer openly for the money entrusted to them.
records.brief: A three-slot contribution box supplying a medicine bottle and a household coin purse.

records.name: Credit for the Countryside
records.description: Farmers and village tradespeople need loans that can be repaid from honest work. Local credit associations will share risks, publish their terms and keep emergency borrowing from becoming a lifetime of dependence.
records.brief: A village loan chest beside a seed sack and a balance with transparent equal weights.

records.name: Water, Power and Public Works
records.description: Growing towns need dependable water, lighting and transport. Engineers and elected district representatives will agree on common service standards, extend reliable networks and train the crews who must keep them working through every season.
records.brief: A water valve connected to an electric street lamp and a municipal service pipe.

records.name: Prosperity That Reaches Home
records.description: The rebuilding programme must finally reach the households still left behind. Secure homes, steady work and dependable services will become ordinary expectations, with local authorities responsible for carrying prosperity beyond the busiest streets.
records.brief: A lit home window above a full meal bowl and a worker's dependable tool case.

records.name: An Army for the Country
records.description: The army must be able to defend the settlements, roads and livelihoods entrusted to it. A review of unit rolls, stores and training will show what our formations can actually do. From that accounting we can build a force whose duties extend beyond ceremony and personal allegiance.
records.brief: A military stores inspection tray beside a district road map and a defensive helmet.

records.name: Professional Officers
records.description: A commission carries responsibility for supplies, training and the lives of subordinates. Regular staff courses and exercises will give officers a common grounding in those duties. Promotion should recognise demonstrated competence and the ability to keep a unit ready for service.
records.brief: A staff-course measuring compass over a tactical exercise board and promotion exam slate.

records.name: Modern Infantry Equipment
records.description: Infantry cannot depend indefinitely on incompatible weapons and improvised replacement parts. Comparative trials will identify practical rifles and squad equipment that our workshops can maintain. The results will inform both procurement and the drills used to train their crews.
records.brief: Two rifle actions compared in a fitted trial rack beside standard replacement parts.

records.name: Engineers and Field Medics
records.description: A damaged crossing or an untreated wound can end a campaign as surely as enemy fire. We will organise specialist training for engineers and medical detachments, and test equipment suited to their work. These companies must be able to move and serve alongside the infantry.
records.brief: A field medic's bag beside a portable bridge section and engineer's shovel.

records.name: Expand the Arsenal
records.description: A dependable arsenal needs gauges, inspection benches and workers who understand the equipment they produce. New military workshops will expand our capacity to manufacture and repair weapons. Artillery trials will help ensure that future orders suit the army we can maintain.
records.brief: An arsenal inspection bench with a barrel gauge and a field-gun breech.

records.name: A Permanent Supply Service
records.description: Each formation must know where its next delivery will come from and how to request it. A permanent supply service will standardise inventories, loading schedules and the maintenance of transport. Trials of motor vehicles and specialist logistics equipment will turn these plans into usable field procedures.
records.brief: A loaded supply truck beneath a depot scheduling clock, counted cargo in its bed.

records.name: A Staff That Works Together
records.description: Infantry officers, engineers, medical staff and quartermasters need to plan the same campaign. Joint exercises will test how their work fits together and reveal where orders fail to reach the units that need them. A shared staff system will preserve those lessons for the next mobilisation.
records.brief: A planning board linking an infantry marker, medical bag and supply route through one coordinated diagram.

records.name: Rebuild the Borderlands
records.description: Eyrie's recovery begins with work that cannot wait for a settlement abroad. We will appoint local repair crews, inventory public buildings and give district officials the authority to keep essential services running.
records.brief: A borderland public building supported by repair scaffolding and a local crew's tool chest.

records.name: Fair Grain Markets
records.description: Uncertain weights, spoiled stores and arbitrary charges leave farming households with little of what they earn. Common market rules and shared storage will ease rural poverty and help local savings find their way into civilian industry.
records.brief: A grain measure balanced against calibrated weights beneath a weatherproof storage roof.

records.name: Roads to Market
records.description: A harvest is worth little when it cannot reach the mill. In Verenia and Eyrie, carriers know which bridge will fail in the rain and which road disappears beneath the thaw. Their accounts will guide the drainage crews and bridge builders, so that a farmer can promise a delivery without first guessing the weather.
records.brief: A harvest wagon crossing a drained all-weather bridge above a swollen stream.

records.name: Process the Harvest at Home
records.description: Milling, preserving and packing should provide skilled work close to the farms. Too much of the harvest leaves Eyrie's villages unprocessed, and too much of its value stays with distant buyers. Local processing works will let farming families sell goods that can travel farther and keep through the winter.
records.brief: A millstone beside sealed produce jars and a packing crate.

records.name: Equipment Cooperatives
records.description: Smallholders cannot each maintain an expensive workshop. Equipment cooperatives will pool their orders, keep spare parts in common stores and repair tools between harvests. A broken machine should bring a mechanic to the farm, not a creditor to the farmhouse.
records.brief: A shared tractor repair bench with pooled spare gears and a farm-tool rack.

records.name: Work Between Harvests
records.description: Seasonal work should not mean seasonal hunger. District offices will match willing workers to processing plants and repair jobs outside the harvest months. More dependable household incomes will reduce poverty further and strengthen confidence in the rebuilding programme.
records.brief: A seasonal calendar wheel connecting a harvest sickle to winter workshop tools.

records.name: Evening Classes
records.description: Schoolrooms can serve adults after the day's work is done. A new programme of reading, arithmetic and technical drawing will reach those whom ordinary schooling has missed and make practical study a lasting part of village life.
records.brief: A night-school slate with arithmetic counters beneath a shaded evening lamp.

records.name: Science for Everyday Work
records.description: Our new classes and processing workshops need instructors who can test a material, explain a circuit and record an experiment. Modest teaching laboratories will strengthen a still-limited scientific base and prepare the ground for electrical research.
records.brief: A teaching circuit connected to a test bulb beside labelled-by-shape material samples.

records.name: District Laboratories
records.description: The district schools have begun borrowing instruments from the workshops, whose foremen now bring their own questions to the teachers. Shared laboratories will give this exchange a permanent home. Materials can be tested, circuits assembled and failed experiments kept on record, instead of each instructor having to begin again alone.
records.brief: A shared laboratory cabinet opened to electrical instruments borrowed from a workshop.

records.name: Technical Fellowships
records.description: Our instructors cannot build a scientific community in the hours left after marking exercise books. Paid fellowships will let promising researchers devote themselves to a difficult problem and bring apprentices into the work. The workshops that supply their instruments will expect useful answers, but must learn to allow time for an honest experiment.
records.brief: A dedicated research bench with a stipend coin tray and an apprentice's spare stool.

records.name: Teachers for Every District
records.description: A village school cannot depend on whichever clerk has an afternoon to spare. Residential courses will prepare teachers to lead a classroom, keep useful records and return to their districts with colleagues they can call upon.
records.brief: A residential teacher-college doorway with a packed teaching satchel and classroom bell.

records.description: The rebuilding programme must finally reach the households still left behind. Secure homes, steady work and dependable services will become ordinary expectations, with local authorities responsible for carrying prosperity beyond the busiest streets.
records.brief: A village doorstep with a delivery basket, sound roof beam and steady lamp.

records.name: A Defensive Service
records.description: Defending Eyrie requires clear duties, dependable training and officers who know the ground. We will review local defence plans and use practical exercises to establish a common standard of service.
records.brief: A local terrain model beneath a defensive service helmet and exercise whistle.

records.name: A Skilled Reserve
records.description: Soldiers returning to civilian life should not have to choose between a livelihood and their place in the reserve. Workshop apprenticeships will give them trades, while refresher courses keep former comrades accustomed to serving together. Employers and officers must agree on a calendar that does not summon a worker away whenever an order comes due.
records.brief: A workshop calendar dividing reserve drills from paid work beside a stored service pack.

records.name: A Field Engineer Corps
records.description: Drainage, covered positions and sound fieldworks matter more than grand plans drawn far from the border. A permanent cadre of engineers will teach units to entrench quickly and guide the development of better engineering equipment.
records.brief: A covered trench cross-section with drainage pipe and engineer's spade.

records.name: Repair Arsenals
records.description: A rifle awaiting a minor repair is still a rifle missing from its unit. Armourers need benches, gauges and a dependable supply of replacement parts. A properly equipped arsenal will let them mend worn weapons before another regiment has to march with whatever happens to be left in the stores.
records.brief: An armourer's vise gripping a worn rifle bolt, repaired parts ready beside it.

records.name: Organise the Supply Depots
records.description: The quartermaster knows what his ledger contains; the driver knows what actually reached the depot. Too often their accounts describe different consignments. A permanent depot service will reconcile receipts, maintain transport schedules and make someone answer for supplies lost between the warehouse and the unit that needed them.
records.brief: A depot cargo crate being matched to a receipt grid and a delivery clock.

records.name: Practical Infantry Drills
records.description: Small units must be able to hold a position, cover a withdrawal and use their weapons effectively. Regular field exercises will reveal shortcomings in our infantry equipment and give instructors experience they can pass on.
records.brief: Infantry practice markers covering a withdrawal route behind a small field barricade.

records.name: Border Observation Sections
records.description: Local knowledge is useful only when a report arrives clearly and in time. Trained observation sections will compare patrol reports, keep accurate sketches and develop better reconnaissance methods for the troops guarding the border.
records.brief: An observation telescope above a sketched ridge line and a patrol notebook.

records.name: A Common Signals Network
records.description: A patrol's warning is useless if headquarters reads it after the reserve has marched the wrong way. Observers, depot staff and reserve officers will practise exchanging the same reports through trained signallers. The message must remain intelligible from the first field notebook to the last unit waiting for orders.
records.brief: A field telephone cable linking a lookout instrument to a reserve muster bell.

records.name: Three Seals, One Constitution
records.description: Katrina's Intergigantes has brought the Houses from rivalry to friendship. Its next task is to prepare a united Verenia. Begin with separate signatures on a common charter, so that courts, accounts and public offices can earn the authority a single country will need. The Houses retain their governments during this first settlement; the constitutional convention will decide how those powers pass to a common government.
records.brief: Three separate metal clasps fitted along one provisional charter binding, each still independently fastened.

records.name: Two Legible Copies
records.description: An agreement is of little use when its readers disagree about what it asks of them. A professional translation office can produce reliable common records and make technical knowledge more accessible, at a continuing administrative cost. Locally appointed clerks can instead draw on familiar voices and existing relationships. Neither arrangement can settle every cultural division within Avian, but both can give its common business a more dependable language.
records.brief: Two parallel diagrammed record sheets beneath a translator's magnifying lens and paired bookmarks.

records.name: The Towns Have Their Own Questions
records.description: A congress agenda can give every House a seat while leaving the towns outside the door. Invite carriers, workshop representatives and local authorities to describe where cooperation would change their working day. Their petitions will inform our construction methods and expose promises that have not yet acquired a responsible office. Peace must become usable beyond the reception room.
records.brief: A town-hall hearing bell beside a carrier's wheel and a workshop petition box.

records.name: The First Constitutional Charter
records.description: Submit the charter to Erie and Eyrie, then seek Avian's own ratification. Common courts and services will be the first institutions of the future Verenia. Their present jurisdiction must be explicit, and each House must accept its obligations. This provisional division of powers gives the later convention an enforceable foundation for a common treasury, citizenship and government.
records.brief: An open charter binder with three equal ratification tabs and a jurisdiction diagram.

records.name: Contributions by Consent
records.description: Avian's treasurer has drawn up three columns, but only one government can promise the sums in the first. Katrina will send Erie and Eyrie the proposed accounts and ask what each is prepared to contribute. Shared roads and workshops need dependable funding; a courteous reply cannot pay a supplier, and a blank signature cannot become a debt.
records.brief: Three contribution trays, one filled and two awaiting replies, beside a common works estimate.

records.name: The Work Between the Houses
records.description: A road crossing a border brings different specifications, maintenance records and suppliers into the same undertaking. Put the charter's shared technical services to work on those differences and give Avian's engineers opportunities to improve industrial methods. Coordination can make future construction more useful without giving our offices the right to order work on another House's land.
records.brief: Two differently built road sections joined by a shared surveying straightedge.

records.name: A Staff with Agreed Limits
records.description: The common staff should know both what its officers can arrange and what requires a further political decision. Develop shared planning, improve support methods and give Avian's officers experience of working with their counterparts. These practical preparations do not themselves create a military alliance or place the other armies under our command.
records.brief: A staff map bounded by a clearly drawn jurisdiction frame, with a telephone outside its limit.

records.name: The Host Before the Court
records.description: Hosting a congress cannot exempt Avian from the rules agreed within it. Katrina will acknowledge the common court's jurisdiction in the matters entrusted to it, including disputes involving her own administration. More reliable records and communications can help the institutions do their work. Their authority must reach the office that supplies the meeting room.
records.brief: A courtroom balance weighing the host administration's own office key.

records.name: Read the Budget as Signed
records.description: The treasurer must turn the Houses' replies into a programme he can actually fund. Some proposed works may have to wait; others can proceed with fewer partners. Katrina will have the signed obligations read beside the estimates. The charter's credibility now depends on an account that neither conceals a refusal nor spends a contribution nobody promised.
records.brief: A budget abacus beside funded construction models and one deferred bridge section.

records.name: The Levy Nobody Authorised
records.description: An emergency circular demands timber, metalwork and transport beyond the contributions the Houses agreed. Its author has attached the congress seal where the suppliers expected a warrant. Katrina must answer for an office acting in her name. If the host can enlarge an obligation whenever its stores run low, every signature beneath the charter becomes a promise made on someone else's terms.
records.brief: A supply requisition hook pulling timber beyond a marked allocation line, a broken budget clasp below.

records.name: Make the Exemptions Real
records.description: The suppliers who planned around their exemptions need more than a corrected circular. Let Avian's works offices bring them orders they can fulfil without surrendering the materials promised to other customers. We shall support civilian industry and better building methods, putting our own resources behind the obligations we accepted. A workshop should be able to plan its next season without wondering whether the host will confiscate its output.
records.brief: An untouched exempt materials stack beside a newly paid civilian workshop order.

records.name: Workshops That Can Plan Ahead
records.description: Reliable orders let workshops exchange methods without wondering whether their next consignment will be seized as an emergency contribution. Bring engineers and production specialists together to pursue improvements in industrial technique. Their research will strengthen Avian's capacity to cooperate through practical knowledge and predictable civilian work.
records.brief: Two engineers' gauges comparing a finished machine component on a shared workbench.

records.name: Defence Under Civil Authority
records.description: The common staff needs officers who can work together and engineers who can maintain the same defences. Train them under the charter's civilian authority. The present commands remain responsible for their forces while the convention prepares the laws and appropriations needed for a unified army. Avian's experience will help turn coordination into a service of the future state.
records.brief: A civilian appropriation box above a coordinated defensive sand table and an engineer's tool.

records.name: Minutes That Can Be Read Outside
records.description: Publish the levy dispute, its resolution and the obligations that remain. The towns must be able to judge how the first common institutions have used their powers before they are asked to entrust more to a united government. These records will accompany our delegates to the constitutional convention.
records.brief: An open minutes stand displaying a clear allocation diagram beside an unlocked public reading-room door.

records.name: A Mandate for United Verenia
records.description: The charter has survived a dispute over money and authority. Its courts can bind the host, its offices can publish honest accounts, and its workshops can plan beyond a season. Conclude this first settlement and open a constituent convention. The next negotiations will establish common institutions and choose the government that will bring the Houses into one country. Avian can seek that responsibility under the same ratified constitution.
records.brief: A provisional charter binding beside an opened convention doorway, the next constitutional stage still ahead.

records.name: Neighbours Without a Common Chair
records.description: The charter negotiations have not produced a common government all can accept. Preserve the friendship already concluded and turn the practical knowledge gathered during the talks towards construction. Katrina can continue to mediate between independent neighbours without treating their refusal as ingratitude. Another congress may become possible; the peace need not wait for it.
records.brief: Three independent neighbour gates connected by a maintained road, an empty congress chair set aside.

records.name: The Avian Question
records.description: Our settlement with the other duchy does not settle Avian's future. Katrina's Intergigantes government has already made cooperation its policy; a government committed to true neutrality has chosen the opposite. Our council must address the Avian question in its own right, not append it to the old family quarrel.
records.brief: An Avian border key resting between an open negotiation case and a closed neutrality gate.

records.name: From Association to Administration
records.description: The duchies now share a government. Avian's accession needs working instructions: common customs documents, recognition of municipal law, and a place for its colleges in the public budget. Once these are ready, Katrina's council will receive the act that ends separate sovereignty.
records.brief: A customs balance beside an Avian municipal key and a college instrument, accession arrangements.

records.name: Close the Third Frontier
records.description: Consent has been given and the transition has run its course. Avian's regiments will enter the common army, its courts the common system of appeals, and its towns the same political country as their neighbours. The treaty becomes a constitution in practice.
records.brief: Three administrative keys placed into one constitutional lock, an Avian service kit joining the common rack.

Our council must address the Avian question in its own right, not append it to the old family quarrel.

records.description: The duchies now share a government. records.brief: A reconciled tariff abacus beside an Avian court appeal case and a college book.

records.description: Consent has been given and the transition has run its course. Avian's regiments will enter the common army, its courts the common system of appeals, and its towns the same political country as their neighbours. The treaty becomes a constitution in practice.
records.brief: An Avian court key joining a common appeals cabinet beside a unified army supply chest.

records.name: The First Common Budget
records.description: The border disappeared from the map before it disappeared from the ledgers. Two offices pay for one school, while neither accepts responsibility for the next. The government must decide who spends the common revenue and who answers to those who supplied it.
records.brief: Two overlapping school payment trays reorganised into one treasury counting board.

records.name: Citizens Beyond the Old Seals
records.description: A subject of the neighbouring House is no longer a foreigner, yet the clerk still demands a special fee. The old courts disagree over inheritance, debt and the right to practise a trade. One shared coat of arms is not enough: residents need dependable protection on both sides of the former border.
records.brief: A common court threshold with a trade licence token and a removed foreign-resident toll chain.

records.name: Homes Beyond the Former Border
records.description: Hired workers sleep in workshop annexes while empty estate houses stand boarded up for years. Municipal builders will receive contracts for homes, wells and drains. The return to ordinary life must reach beyond the main square.
records.brief: Boarded estate shutters opened beside a new workers' house and a drainage pipe.

records.name: Treatment Without a Ducal Certificate
records.description: Patients are asked where they came from, then sent to another district for a certificate. Physicians propose common sanitary rules, recognition of training and a shared supply list for rural clinics. Disease never respected the borders, even when the dukes did.
records.brief: A rural clinic medicine cabinet paired with a common diagnostic kit and a removed district barrier.

records.name: Roads to a Common Market
records.description: Roads once led to checkpoints and garrisons rather than neighbouring towns. Carriers now mark damaged bridges, dangerous slopes and needless detours on a single map. Their markings will become the first common road plan.
records.brief: A route map showing a direct repaired bridge replacing a checkpoint detour, with survey dividers.

records.name: Machine Shops Instead of Tollhouses
records.description: The old customs warehouses stand beside useful roads but hold little beyond broken barriers. Craftsgriffons propose machine tools and repair shops. Orders will connect suppliers from different districts, turning the removal of the border into the beginning of new work.
records.brief: A disused customs warehouse converted into a machine shop, its old barrier leaning outside.

records.name: One Drawing for Different Workshops
records.description: A bolt made in one district will not fit a nut from another. Masters regard their own measurements as part of their craft's dignity. A common standards office will leave their makers' marks intact, but insist that parts fit without a file.
records.brief: A threaded nut sliding cleanly onto a bolt beneath a standards gauge.

records.name: Evening Classes
records.description: A new school will not help an adult read a contract if its doors open only during working hours. Teachers and workshops will arrange evening lessons. Their pupils have tired claws and too much experience to be ashamed of their first page.
records.brief: A work apron hung beside a lit school desk carrying an illustrated contract lesson.

records.name: The Verenian Institute of Applied Studies
records.description: Each former capital has its teachers, workshops and collection of instruments. Separately they request the same books and fail to finish the same experiments. A shared institute will begin with exchanged equipment, open admissions and the right to argue with a colleague from another House.
records.brief: Two borrowed scientific instruments meeting beneath a shared institute arch.

records.name: Serving One Country
records.description: Regimental rolls still remember whom the militia once assembled to fight. Common service requires more than a new cockade: shared appointments, training and accountability to civil government. Officers must decide what will sustain the defence of a small country.
records.brief: A common appointment rack holding aligned service batons under a civilian budget clasp.

records.name: Reserves of the Common Country
records.description: The old arsenals were designed for a short campaign over a neighbouring hill. The common country needs repair stocks, dispersed depots and workshops able to replace a lost delivery. An order cannot make us a great power, but we need not depend on a single road.
records.brief: Three dispersed repair-stock sheds linked by alternate roads around one blocked route.

records.name: An Account to All Verenia
records.description: The first common projects are complete. Not every letter to the capital is grateful: contractors dispute prices, communities dispute priorities and treasurers dispute missing receipts. A published account must name both the promises fulfilled and those paid for work left undone.
records.brief: An audit balance weighing paid coins against one finished beam and one unfinished fitting.

records.name: The Country the Morning After
records.description: Unification will be remembered for its speeches and raised flag. Its durability will be decided later: whether medicine reaches a village, a diploma is recognised in the next town, and a court hears a complaint against its own official. We need a country that keeps working when the celebration is over.
records.brief: A village medicine delivery beside a recognised diploma book and an accessible courthouse key.

records.name: The Price of Victory
records.description: Vincent's supporters speak readily of the inheritance victory will bring. They speak less often of the farms that must sustain it and the promises the duke will owe afterwards. Choosing this campaign means abandoning the negotiated settlement with Eyrie: Verenia is to be united by force, and Erie will have to govern the consequences. Officers, suppliers and patrons must state what they expect before the first regiment marches.
records.brief: A campaign sword laid across a farm's grain account and a patron's credit chest.

records.name: Promises in Writing
records.description: A campaign draws on credit as well as courage. Carriers advance their wagons, suppliers reserve their stock, and influential households expect their service to count when rewards are considered. Vincent will require clear undertakings and a supply service capable of keeping them. Loyalty deserves an answer; it cannot be allowed to write its own unlimited claim upon the defeated.
records.brief: A wagon harness beside a bound supply undertaking with a diagrammed delivery schedule.

records.name: Not a Dowry
records.description: Rosaline Erie of Bantry has discovered that her name makes a convenient ending to other people's speeches. A union between Houses, they suggest, could be made complete through her. She intends to speak for herself. Vincent must hear her objection before anyone turns a personal correspondence into a marriage settlement or presents another griffon's future as part of the spoils.
records.brief: An unsealed personal letter protected from an estate-transfer chain; no bridal symbols.

records.name: The Final Ultimatum
records.description: Vincent will put Erie's claim behind a final demand upon Eyrie. The document cannot make his inheritance more certain than Iovinus's, but it can prepare the grounds on which he intends to fight. Existing promises of peace must still be honoured. Sending the demand leaves the decision to begin a war, and responsibility for that decision, with the duke.
records.brief: A closed ultimatum case beside a poised but still sheathed sword at the frontier.

records.name: Terms for the Defeated
records.description: The military result is settled. Now the people of the defeated districts must discover what Vincent's victory means at a workshop door or in a dispute over a field. Local charters could protect rights his own followers must respect. Ducal commissioners could instead organise the settlement under his direct authority. Either course will make demands that a proclamation of triumph can conceal only briefly.
records.brief: A district office key between a local court bench and a commissioner's command desk.

records.name: The Districts' Own Rights
records.description: A promise of local rights must be usable by someone who opposed Erie. Let the districts retain recognised procedures for their property, public works and complaints, with obligations the duke's officers must also observe. Building through these institutions will take patience. It will give a town reason to repair its future without first finding a patron at Vincent's court.
records.brief: A municipal charter lock shielding a property key from a nearby military sword.

records.name: The Duke's Commissioners
records.description: Vincent will place reconstruction under commissioners who answer directly to him. They can bring scattered industrial work into a common programme and make orders reach their destination quickly. Their authority will also make every intrusion the duke's own. The defeated districts may comply without feeling represented, and efficiency will have to bear the weight of that distinction.
records.brief: A commissioner's dispatch cabinet connecting district workshop orders to one ducal desk.

records.name: The First Petition
records.description: A family from the defeated districts claims an estate sought by one of Vincent's wartime patrons. The patron can prove his service; the family can produce evidence that its property was never his to receive. The first difficult hearing will reveal whether the new order can distinguish a debt owed by the duke from a debt imposed on someone else.
records.brief: A family house key balanced against a patron's campaign medal, with a surveyed estate plan beneath.

records.name: Work Beyond the Victory Parade
records.description: The estate decision has travelled further than its authors expected. Builders and workshop owners now judge new offers against what they have learned about the settlement. Put civilian investment behind the reconstruction contracts and give industrial specialists work worth improving. A durable peace requires people to risk their savings on something other than the favour of the next victorious officer.
records.brief: A reconstruction contract board showing a building plan beside paid materials and a workshop saw.

records.name: A Levy That Can Be Maintained
records.description: Wartime service cannot remain a succession of personal bargains. Establish regular training and reliable equipment for the troops, with obligations that can be understood beyond a patron's household. The men who fought for Erie need to know what their service now requires. The districts expected to sustain them need an answer more definite than the continuation of an emergency.
records.brief: A regular training clock above standard service kits, replacing loose personal pledge cords.

records.name: Reconcile the Civil Registers
records.description: The victorious court cannot govern two duchies from incompatible tax rolls and contradictory property registers. Surveyors, clerks and engineers will reconcile the records before the new administration claims the right to speak for every district.
records.brief: Two conflicting land-survey grids aligned beneath a chancery ruler; this is domestic consolidation, not Avian conquest.
records.lore_notes: Historical ID is misleading: current name, description and electronics reward concern reconciling the two duchies' civil registers, not invading Avian.

records.name: A Duke Bound by His Word
records.description: Vincent will make the district guarantees binding upon his own rule. If he protected his patron's estate award, that exception must now be withdrawn and the claim returned to an evidentiary hearing. Where he already upheld the hearing, its principle must endure beyond one case. The charters can become the foundation of his settlement only if they reach the hand that signed them.
records.brief: A ducal office key caught within a judicial measuring frame beside a reopened estate case.

records.name: A Single Chancery
records.description: Bring the commissioners into a lasting ducal administration. Industry and the army will answer through a common chain, giving Vincent greater power to carry his decisions through. The estate judgement already made will remain part of that order. Central authority can protect a fair hearing or preserve a patron's advantage; it makes the duke responsible for whichever precedent he keeps.
records.brief: A single chancery dispatch chute feeding factory and army order trays.

records.name: What the Next Generation Receives
records.description: The children growing up under Vincent's settlement will inherit more than the story of a battle. They will inherit the answer given to a dispossessed family, the limits placed on a supporter and the habits of the offices that govern them. Let the old military rivalry end without pretending that victory has erased its consequences or decided Avian's future.
records.brief: A repaired district school doorway above a laid-down campaign sword and protected property key.

records.name: The Third Banner
records.description: Avian's council has chosen true neutrality and rejected the work between the giants. Vincent's settlement with Eyrie leaves that frontier outside the common country. His commanders propose a campaign to bring Avian into the same realm. This is a new hostile demand, not a right secretly awarded by a family treaty. Existing pacts must be honoured or ended openly.
records.brief: A neutral Avian frontier gate facing a new military demand case; no suggestion of treaty consent.

records.name: The Avian Articles
records.description: An Avian registrar arrives with the old assessments and a list of families whose property has already been promised to two different officers. Vincent has heard this dispute before. The third House must receive a settlement it can actually live under: protected local courts and property, or a commission for which the duke accepts direct responsibility. Victory does not choose between them.
records.brief: An Avian property register with two competing claim tabs beside a local court key.

records.name: A Third Seat at the Table
records.description: The first Avian accounts have survived comparison with the treasury's ledgers. Workshops have contracts and the courts know where their decisions must be sent. Vincent can now abolish the provisional frontier and give these obligations the force of ordinary government. The third seat at his table represents inhabitants who must be governed, not merely another defeated name.
records.brief: A provisional Avian border barrier dismantled beside a paid workshop account and permanent office key.

records.name: The Price of Vigilance
records.description: Iovinus Eyrie has made readiness a condition of survival. Yet the same emergency orders are renewed, the same villages supply the men, and the same returns promise soldiers an inspection cannot always find. Before choosing accommodation with Erie or a campaign to break its claim, the duke must discover what his vigilance has cost the country, and what his army can actually deliver.
records.brief: A cracked muster drum beside an underfilled equipment rack and a village grain levy basket.

records.name: Security Without the Feud
records.description: Iovinus has guarded the frontier for so long that his officers have begun to confuse its safety with their freedom to raid across it. He will seek a settlement that protects Eyrie without requiring Erie's submission. The muster must be honest, the family must be allowed to speak, and the safeguards must bind both commands. His army will defend the country. It will not answer a failed conference by conquering the neighbour.
records.brief: A sheathed patrol sword resting beneath an independently locked civic gate, restraint without submission.

records.name: The Men Behind the Numbers
records.description: A name on a muster roll may represent a soldier, a discharged veteran or an absence nobody has dared to explain. Iovinus must decide who will ask the questions. Local representatives will want to account for the men their villages sent; an army commission will insist that the inquiry remains a matter of service. Either must begin by counting those who are actually there.
records.brief: A muster counting board with missing counters beside an actual service-kit rack.

records.name: Montague's Crossing
records.description: Montague Eyrie, Earl of Verenia, wants to visit Rosaline Erie of Bantry. His officers see a route through hostile positions; he sees the journey to someone whose company he has missed. Iovinus can secure his passage without dictating its purpose. Let the two speak for themselves. A family connection may open the way to an agreement, but it must not become a marriage imposed to spare the dukes an awkward conversation.
records.brief: A personal envelope and travelling case beside an opened guarded crossing; no wedding iconography.

records.name: Stand Down the Raiding Parties
records.description: The muster has been examined, Montague has opened a personal way across the divide, and the safeguards are ready. Iovinus can now order his officers to put away the excuses by which every raid becomes a precaution. The same restraint will bind Erie. This armistice is the foundation of a permanent settlement, not a year's holiday from the feud.
records.brief: Two patrol lanterns extinguished beside a permanently raised frontier arm.

records.name: Roads Between the Houses
records.description: The engineers have spent years marking bridges for demolition. Now they must discover which can carry ordinary traffic again. Survey the approaches, compare the available materials and make the frontier routes usable without an army preparing their passage. The same practical knowledge will serve our own roads and the settlement we are building with Erie.
records.brief: A demolition charge removed from a bridge beneath a surveyor's measuring rod.

records.name: Safeguards That Bind Us Too
records.description: The muster tells Iovinus what his army can do. Montague's journey reminds him that not every crossing must be an operation. Before concluding an armistice, he must decide what will make its promises credible: mixed patrols empowered to question both commands, or a restitution fund that acknowledges damage and hears property claims. Either course asks the duke to restrain his own supporters. Only then can he ask the same of Vincent.
records.brief: A public rules board bearing patrol-route diagrams beside a restitution purse.

records.name: Friendship with Safeguards
records.description: An open crossing has made the frontier's old habits harder to defend. The treaty will end the official rivalry and relinquish the territorial demands that let either House call its neighbour's independence a provocation. Iovinus retains his army and his government. He gains a peace that no longer needs the prospect of victory to justify itself.
records.brief: Two territorial claim stakes withdrawn behind a preserved pair of independent gates.

records.name: Where Command Ends
records.description: A reliable army needs a clear account of what it may demand from the country it protects. Local councils want a voice when a requisition takes away their last wagon. The officers answer that a command cannot negotiate every order with a village meeting. Iovinus must establish who will hear an objection, and whose duty it will be to make the army respect the answer.
records.brief: A village cart stopped beside a military requisition desk and an appeals bell.

records.name: An Intergigantes Association
records.description: Intergigantes has brought Avian out of isolation. Iovinus can now offer more than an observer's chair: a negotiated place in a united Verenia. Begin with the courts, colleges and municipal charters. A separate accession act will decide who governs the common country, and Katrina must be able to read it before she signs.
records.brief: An empty observer's chair moved toward a negotiation table, a separate Avian invitation on its seat.
